points: Mine Production In 2024, global silver mine production rose by 0.9 percent to 819.7 Moz, underpinned by increased output from lead/zinc mines in Australia and the recovery of supply from Mexico, as Newmont’s Peñasquito mine returned to full production.
Lower output from Chile, down 8.8 Moz y/y, partially offset this growth.
In contrast, silver production from gold mines recorded the strongest growth, up 12% y/y to 13.9 Moz, a three-year high.
Recycling Recycling rose 6 percent in 2024, reaching a 12-year high of 193.9 Moz.
In percentage terms, the highest gain came from silverware recycling, which climbed by 11 percent as firmer silver prices and cost-of-living issues encouraged selling in Western markets.
Silver Demand Total silver demand fell by 3 percent to 1.16 billion ounces (Boz) in 2024.
Silverware demand in 2023 fell by 25 percent to 55.2 Moz.
Silver Jewelry and Silverware Silver jewelry fabrication grew by 3 percent to 208.7 Moz in 2024.
Improving exports to key Western countries also lifted fabrication in Thailand by 13 percent.
Silverware demand declined by 2 percent to a three-year low of 54.2 Moz.
Between 1500 and 1800, Bolivia, Peru and Mexico accounted for over 85 percent of world silver production and trade as it bolstered Spanish influence in the New World and elsewhere.
Silver production continued to expand worldwide, growing from 40 to 80 million ounces annually by the 1870s.
Production over the last quarter of the 19th century quadrupled over the average of the first 75 years to a total of nearly 120 million ounces annually.
The twenty years between 1900 and 1920 resulted in a 50 % increase in global production, and brought the total to about 190 million ounces annually.
